Q: Is CPU allowed to perform a speculative execution on nullptr branch conditions? A:

All modern x86 CPUs use VIPT L1d caches, so the tag uses the high bits of the physical address and does have to wait for the TLB result. A VIPT cache that's small and associative enough behaves like PIPT not VIVT.

(Some AMD CPUs use way-prediction and micro-tagging, so they could maybe speculate on which cached data to return? I don't know if that's a thing.)

The Meltdown vuln is when you get a TLB hit (and an L1d hit), so data actually is returned as an input to later instructions. But the load is marked as faulting (so it can't actually retire) because the CPU is currently in user mode, but the TLB entry is only valid for kernel mode. To fix this in hardware, presumably the load unit also masks the data result to 0 as well as marking the load uop as faulting if it reaches retirement, so speculative exec uses a boring constant 0 instead of secret data potentially as an index to future cache misses which could create a cache-timing attack. (There might be other ways to fix it, I don't know what Intel actually uses, but this seems like the obvious fix to me, if that doesn't make critical path gate-delay a problem.)

Meltdown is about reading kernel pages from user-space using its actual address, not random cache lines from the zero address. Various MDS vulnerabilities are more like that, though, using values floating around in internal buffers that speculatively end up in registers after various faults.

But other than that brain-fart, your other comments in this Q&A about speculative execution are correct. Yeah, everything is speculative, but the CPU doesn't actually take an exception until a faulting instruction reaches retirement (i.e. becomes non-speculative). This is how they ignore speculative faults.

(Some things like software-prefetch of a bad pointer can be slow if it causes a page-walk. That's one reason why the Linux kernel doesn't use SW prefetch while traversing linked lists: being slow at the terminating NULL often costs more than any savings.)

Q: Why does a call to `ref` on a reference to `substr` produce "LVALUE"? A:

With \substr(...) you did take a reference to a modifiable memory location, since substr() is an lvalue-function, and your $lv prints LVALUE(memory-location). The LVALUE is a reference to a special type of scalar so ref (and Scalar::Util::reftype) return that label. The memory location contains what substr(...) (would have) returned.

When you print $$lv you get what your substr() call returned, and if you assign to $$lv the original string's corresponding range of characters is changed (since substr is a function that can be used as lvalue).

A command-line program ("one-liner") as an example:

perl -wE'$s = "hello"; $lv = \substr($s, 1, 2); say $lv; say $$lv; 
         $$lv = "WHOA"; say $s'

(I split it into two lines for eaiser reading. In Bash one can still just copy-paste into terminal)

It prints

LVALUE(0x55d494b604d8)
el
hWHOAlo

Once we have that LVALUE reference in $lv we can continue using it -- further writes to $$lv change the original string

perl -wE'$s = "hello"; $lv = \substr($s, 1, 2); 
         for (qw(WHOA A OHYES)) { $$lv = $_; say $s }'

Prints

hWHOAlo
hAlo
hOHYESlo

Q: How to copy, paste and flip horizontally and vertically many images? A:

You can do this more simply with ImageMagick. Load the image, make a copy, rotate the copy 180 and then composite the two images together, selecting the lightest pixel at each location in the image:

magick cwxAr.png \( +clone -rotate 180 \) -compose lighten -composite result.png

Q: Modify gcc gcov counter size A:

Don't modify GCC — use a different instrumentation pass instead.

GCC's --coverage (i.e. -fprofile-arcs -ftest-coverage) really does hard-code 8-byte counters per arc, and the existing answer is correct that changing that requires patching GCC. But coverage isn't the only instrumentation pass GCC ships with, and one of the others is far cheaper if you only need line/block hit-or-miss (no execution counts, no branch counts).

Why GCC won't ship a 1-bit option: gcov's counters aren't only for coverage — they're also the data source for -fprofile-use (PGO). PGO uses arc counts to weight branch predictions, drive __builtin_expect defaults, and decide hot/cold function placement. A 1-bit "did this branch fire at least once" tells PGO nothing useful — it can't distinguish a branch hit a million times from one hit once. Smaller-counter proposals (1-byte, 1-bit) have surfaced on the GCC mailing list but never landed because the dual-purpose design ties their hands. This is exactly why GCC ships a separate sanitizer-coverage pass for the coverage-only / fuzzing case.

-fsanitize-coverage=trace-pc (GCC 6+, also in Clang) inserts a single call to a user-supplied callback at the start of every basic block:

void __sanitizer_cov_trace_pc(void) __attribute__((no_instrument_function));

You implement that callback. The simplest implementation marks a bit in a fixed bitmap and returns:

#define BITMAP_BYTES 16384  /* 128 Kbits — pick whatever fits your RAM */
static unsigned char hit_bitmap[BITMAP_BYTES];

__attribute__((no_instrument_function, no_sanitize("coverage")))
void __sanitizer_cov_trace_pc(void) {
    /* Use the return address as the basic-block ID. */
    uintptr_t pc = (uintptr_t)__builtin_return_address(0);
    uint32_t idx = (pc >> 2) & ((BITMAP_BYTES * 8) - 1);
    hit_bitmap[idx >> 3] |= 1u << (idx & 7);
}

no_instrument_function and no_sanitize("coverage") keep the callback itself from being instrumented (otherwise it'd recurse on every entry).

You then dump hit_bitmap to the host (over serial, JTAG, whatever) and decode each set bit back to a source location by walking the ELF's __sancov_pcs section + DWARF line info.

RAM comparison for a typical small project:

Approach Per-instrumentation-point cost
--coverage (gcov) 8 bytes (one 64-bit counter per arc)
-fsanitize-coverage=trace-pc with hash bitmap 1 bit (with collisions tunable by bitmap size)
-fsanitize-coverage=trace-pc with exact bitmap 1 bit per call site, no collisions

For an embedded project with a few thousand instrumentation points, the gcov path needs ~24-50 KB of RAM; trace-pc with a 16 KB hash bitmap covers any project size at the cost of a small false-positive rate (N_sites / N_bits per check).

What you give up: trace-pc is hit/miss only — no execution counts, no per-branch coverage. If your reports rely on those, you need gcov (or a hybrid). For "did this code path run during my tests?" coverage, trace-pc is enough.

Turnkey implementation: I maintain pio-cov, a PlatformIO library that ships both backends — gcov via a host-replay protocol over serial (no per-file device buffer; ~96 bytes BSS regardless of project size) and trace-pc with three sub-backends (hash / dense / indexed) trading RAM against collision rate. The trace-pc path is the direct answer to your question.
